proposals.label: AI partnership with the Global South
proposals.definition: AI as part of partnership, sharing and democratization agendas with developing countries.
proposals.inclusion: Passages promising AI cooperation, sharing tools, or democratizing technology for the Global South.
proposals.exclusion: General development assistance not tied to AI or technology.
proposals.boundary_cases: Sharing digital public infrastructure without AI mention does not count.

examples.quote: AI will be very much part of a partnership agenda with the global South.

proposals.label: AI misuse sharpening bias
proposals.definition: Brief warnings that misuse of AI sharpens bias and erodes mutual respect, turning technology from hope into anxiety.
proposals.inclusion: Passages stating AI misuse increases bias, division or anxiety.
proposals.boundary_cases: Could overlap with ethics; code here when the harm is framed as misuse sharpening social or international bias.

examples.quote: Misuse of AI is sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect.

proposals.label: Responsible AI listed among G20 outcomes
proposals.definition: AI named as one item in a list of policy initiatives or concerns without elaboration.
proposals.inclusion: Passages where responsible AI is one entry in a list of summit outcomes or initiatives.
proposals.exclusion: Passages elaborating AI's effects or governance.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the list item is later elaborated in the same passage, code the substantive theme.

examples.text: The New Delhi G20 outcomes are expressed both as larger policies and as specific initiatives. They could be about building cities for tomorrow or fighting corruption; eliminating hunger or delivering quality education; ending plastic pollution or preserving the ocean-based economy; or for that matter, enhancing food security or even mapping global skills. Some address long-standing issues like the gender divide and climate action. Others focus on new concerns, such as the responsible harnessing of artificial intelligence. All in all, we have placed for the world’s consideration a set of actionable propositions, constructive solutions and new directions.

If any of them are undermined, peace will inevitably be weakened. After eight decades of the UN, This should have become our second nature. Instead, what we are actually seeing is a weaponization of everything. A mindset of extreme competition has set in, undermining institutions and establishing choke points. It extends from the world of finance to constricting market access, disrupting supply chains, and withholding technology. Resources and connectivity have become particularly subject to leveraging. As a result, nations are now more focused on de-risking and diversifying. Now, while this may secure their interest to varying degrees, the overall atmosphere is no longer that of trust or goodwill. Mr. President, the predicament of the global South is particularly acute. It faces a 4F crisis of the security of food, fuel, fertilizer, and finance. The combined impact of a super El Nino, compounding fertilizer shortages, and now impediments to grain movements, all these are cause for alarm. Moreover, SDG progress is under increasing pressure. The global South's right to industrialize is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial. The march of technology that was meant to instill hope has now become a source of anxiety. Misuse of AI is sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect. These directions bode ill for the aims and objectives of the United Nations. Governments indulging in such practices must be held accountable. There must be no dilution in our zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism. Its financial aspects, in particular, should be exposed and should be countered. Mr. President, yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this Assembly. As a first responder, we were there early, be it the Nepal flash floods or the Venezuela earthquake. Our limb fitment camps have given a new hope to many across the world. Whether to meet food and medicine shortages, energy or fertilizer needs, or indeed creating livelihoods, India has contributed continuously and will do so. Our capacity building and experience sharing programs have made a real difference across the global South, especially in Africa. The same international spirit also inspires our contribution to safeguarding peace. India has always been at the forefront of UN peacekeeping operations. Right now, our contingents are present in nine out of 11 mandates. Our troops have stood their ground firmly and professionally, even under pressure. We take pride that an Indian woman combat helicopter pilot was awarded the UN 2025 Military Gender Advocate of the Year. Mr. President, new challenges in the maritime domain have added to long-standing ones on land. There have been attacks on commercial shipping and seafarers in the Gulf and from the Red Sea to the Black Sea. Indian seafarers have lost their lives, as indeed have others from other nations. This is completely unacceptable. India has joined Liberia and 23 other partners in an initiative to rally global public opinion against such unwarranted targeting. We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised. Scrupulously observing international law is an integral element of that endeavour. An issue central to current global conversations is that of AI. India hosted the AI Impact Summit this February, gathering together the best minds on that subject. We view AI as a transformational driver for human empowerment, economic prosperity, and population-scale problem solving. We believe in the right of each nation to shape its ecosystem with the development of its own models and deployment strategies consistent with its national goals and priorities. AI will be very much part of a partnership agenda with the global South. As technology is democratized, this process is greatly facilitated, Mr. President, by an ethos of mutual respect.
